Also, it looks like you are calling wakeup neighbours for every type of body, when it is only the KinematicBody that is not working. That could mean doing more work than necessary.

The other problem here could simply be that you are not setting velocity. I wonder if move_and_slide() is working because internally it is properly setting the velocity of the underlying bullet body.

In 4.x, the CharacterBody3D/2D has a velocity property that you can set directly, but for some reason 3.x doesn't seem to have that. 

Perhaps being able to set the velocity properly might fix this wake problem. Most velocity solver engines don't respond well to the user porting around.

If it did fix it, and you did add a `velocity` property to 3.x KinematicBody, then you are just making it more like 4.x, so that doesn't seem bad.

> Also, it looks like you are calling wakeup neighbours for every type of body, when it is only the KinematicBody that is not working. That could mean doing more work than necessary.

I don't think this is actually a problem in practice. All objects should (ideally) be expected to wake up their neighbours when moved via `set_translate()`. `RigidBodies` are 99.9% moved by applying forces, so `set_translate()` is never called, and the wake up code only runs when they are teleported. Which is exactly what we want (I guess it's possible they could "try" to wake up twice on that tick, but they do this anyway every iteration step of physics afaik).

Static body _should_ wakeup when teleported.

Kinematic body _should_ wakeup when teleported, but the only issue remaining here (that I can immediately see) is the duplication between `test_motion` and `set_transform` both going through neighbours to wake up.

It's almost like this `move_and_slide` is the only exception to the rule _always wakeup_. :thinking:

Probably a bit more complex than this and none of my quick attempts at testing it worked. I can look again tomorrow if it is still up in the air. 

I am curious as to exactly what it is that move_and_slide() is doing to make it work, when your transform setting is not.

> I am curious as to exactly what it is that move_and_slide() is doing to make it work, when your transform setting is not.

It's `body_test_motion`, inside there it activates anything it hits. But there's no guarantee that after a `body_test_motion` the next teleport will be to the location that it tested.

> > I am curious as to exactly what it is that move_and_slide() is doing to make it work, when your transform setting is not.
> 
> It's `body_test_motion`, inside there it activates anything it hits. But there's no guarantee that after a `body_test_motion` the next teleport will be to the location that it tested.

Right, I get it now.

I'm also not convinced yet without profiling that it's actually _worth_ adding extra logic to prevent the wakeup. It's pretty cheap it's just going through a short list, which will have just been gone through in `body_test_motion` so should be in cache.

It doesn't actually *do* anything because it has an `if !active` check in there, it's just the cost of iterating the neighbours. So we're really only considering a situation where there's e.g. 1000 objects `move_and_sliding` through a bunch of other rigid bodies, in which case the physics is more likely to be the bottleneck.

The reason I wouldn't want to do rigid_body_wake_neighbours() more than necessary is that it appears to be waking up everything that was hit in broadphase. 

I don't know what bullet does internally, but the optimum approach is to wake up everything you hit after narrow phase (not broadphase). That will wake less objects. 

Godot Physics wakes everything hit in broadphase (which I think is wrong). Jolt Physics does it properly (I think) and wakes up everything that actually collides (narrow phase). I am not sure what bullet does internally. If it acts like Godot Physics, then what you are doing in rigid_body_wake_neighbours() looks like the same thing it would do. If it acts like Jolt, then it would wake only the objects actually hit.
I assume that bullet physics broadphase hits have already tested collision masks and collision layers? So you are not waking anything that you wouldn't actually collide with due to masks?

So that leans us back towards the approach of API, and specifying from the scene side whether we want to do a wakeup, kind of like the original PR.

We either need to assure the physics it _doesn't_ need to wakeup, or we need to explicitly request it. :thinking: 

> I assume that bullet physics broadphase hits have already tested collision masks and collision layers? So you are not waking anything that you wouldn't actually collide with due to masks?

That's already done in Godot Physics via the BVH, but actually no idea in Bullet, let me check. (that would be easy to add though)

UPDATE : Yeah looks like the Bullet broadphase does handle the layers as far as I can see (it rejigs it after changing layer at least, so I assume so).

Anyway, it looks good to me. I dramatically prefer this approach than adding API, and we only have to assure it doesn't do more work than it is going to do anyway. Double waking shouldn't hurt, it's likely just a flag and a tiny bit of logic.

I suspect bullet wakes up on broadphase because I suspect Godot maybe got the idea from there. It should also have run a callback to check masks / layers. 

I have to run for tonight, so will check over that tomorrow, plus any further comments you have made.

So I looked at the idea of saying 'good enough', but then, looking at the new function more carefully, it registered that it is running through the entire global pair list for each call to set_state(TRANSFORM). So even if this doesn't do too much waking, just the traversal itself may be too expensive for this pathway. In 4.x, this is a hot path, which in practice may be called for almost every object every frame even though it shouldn't (not sure about 3.x).

Anyway, just justifying why I wasted another day looking into this ;-).

So I have been stepping through and reading Bullet code and ultimately found this one liner which explains why Bullet is not doing what we would expect: 

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/0719aca15406d41374a9531a0977a04f8b06b8e2/modules/bullet/rigid_body_bullet.cpp#L1074

If you delete this line, the original MRP will work and Kinematic and Static bodies will be set to the default ACTIVE_TAG in their constructor. 

Additionally, if you delete this line, you can also delete the manual wake up code from move_and_slide() and it will still work (however, this is not necessary or particularly beneficial, so I don't see a reason to touch it). 

I don't know why all kinematic and static bodies were having the simulation disabled. Maybe there was a good reason, or maybe it was a misunderstanding of what it means. Bullet knows what a Kinematic and Static body is, so enabling simulation shouldn't do anything much except ensure that things collide and wake properly (I think). 

So I think this is the way to fix it, and I think this should be fixed, but it then does need to be tested. Probably the worst thing that can happen to an active Kinematic object is just that it goes to sleep again (which is how it is starting out currently), so I think it is fine. I can't say for sure that there wouldn't be behavioural changes though. Platformer 3D and Truck Town seem to work.

### What about static body removal

I am not sure if this one liner works for 'wake on static object removal', but if it doesn't, then I reckon static object removal could be a separate PR or fix (if desired).

Looking at the Jolt docs, it appears that Jolt does not wake on static object removal or movement. The Jolt docs tell the user to do it themselves, and I can guess at some good reasons for this. So given that, it may need API consideration to do properly across all platforms, which maybe means a proposal / discussion to make sure that 2D / 3D, Jolt / Godot / Rapier / etc are all on the same page.

Sounds like a good investigation, I'll try this line and have a look, that would be ideal if it's just something that's been turned off.

Looks like it was added in the first PR adding bullet by @AndreaCatania , I don't know if he's still contributing and is unlikely to remember as it's from 9 years ago, but pinging just in case.

I'll try and see if this works, and if there any performance implications. If it does, it's possible we could just combine the two and have the existing logic above wake constraints up when removing a body.

Ok the saga continues.

While the one liner works, we now have the opposite problem - that it appears to wake bodies in the new position, but doesn't wake bodies in the position it has teleported _from_. So it now gives a better result for the moving case, and that alone seems a good reason to use it.

Combined with the call to `awake` when removing a body from the space (that is already in the PR), this also deals with waking bodies on removing from the scene. However the problem of moving a platform directly out of the way is now open again, I'll see if we can solve this too. I'll be away over the weekend so feel free to post any more findings here or on RC. :+1: 

It also doesn't seem to deal with the problem when disabling the collision shape, although I'm pretty sure we can intercept that and call `wake_neighbours`. The moving case is the more tricky one to deal with efficiently.

What we might be able to do is a simple AABB test of the new location and the previous, if they don't overlap then run the full `wake_neighbours`. It's not perfect, but between them it should catch most of the cases.

UPDATE: Actually even better would be to use the "timer" approach I think I mentioned in an earlier post on this thread. Every time we move the `static / kinematic`, we store the current tick. If we try and move it and it has not been moved in the previous tick, we run `wake_neighbours`. This should catch nearly all cases and not impede efficiency for a continuous movement. So together with waking on disable / enable, this should catch all the current bugs I think.

I'll have a look after the weekend and see whether `GodotPhysics` is also affected by any of these and whether we can fix these too (likely in another PR though).

I spent a bit of today reading documentation and stuff and trying out other engine configs. I think this may be a post-weekend thing anyway, but I did learn a bit from PhysX, Bullet Docs, Jolt, etc. Just posting what I can quickly as I have to wrap it up for the night.

We seem to have 3 different scenarios: 

1. 'wake on move into' - Everything but Bullet works (roughly good enough)
2. 'wake on move away from' - Jolt and Bullet and Godot Physics 2D do not work (4.x Godot Physics 3D seems like  it may)
3. 'wake on free' - No configuration works

So if we fix more than 1. then we need to consider fixing it across the board (eventually).

The 'wake on move into' could be done with this one liner, but Bullet docs say you should set a Kinematic object to `DISABLE_DEACTIVATION`. So replacing `DISABLE_SIMULATION` with `DISABLE_DEACTIVATION` seems good. Even better might be to only activate a Kinematic body when it is moving...but that may require trickier code:

PhysX has the best approach I have seen today. This is how I want speculative wakes to work, just waking for a frame or two to see if movement starts (not waking for the full time):

https://nvidia-omniverse.github.io/PhysX/physx/5.8.0/docs/RigidBodyDynamics.html

> For kinematic actors, special sleep rules apply. A kinematic actor is asleep unless a target pose has been set (in which case it will stay awake until two consecutive simulation steps without a target pose being set have passed). As a consequence, it is not allowed to use setWakeCounter() for kinematic actors. The wake counter of a kinematic actor is solely defined based on whether a target pose has been set.

I have more to say but I am running out of time. If you find better ways to solve this more broadly for bullet, that should be helpful, but we will also want to consider Jolt and Godot Physics.

It may make sense to consider the API again and make a specific `WakeNeighbours` function (rather than a flag). However this function could then be used across all physics engines in any scenario where a user is not getting the wake functionality they need. If we used it, it wouldn't be deprecated in future, but rather become the way things should be done. 

The reason to use an explicit function like that would be if we simply can't find a sufficiently performant way to do 'good enough' waking otherwise. Jolt docs tell the user to handle 2. and 3. themselves, but Godot doesn't provide a mechanism for them to do so.

Godot Physics already has a reasonably performant and 'good enough' way to solve the problem (I think), but I am not sure that Jolt or Bullet do. So it gets interesting.

> Even better might be to only activate a Kinematic body when it is moving

I'm not sure if there is any need. A kinematic body doesn't get pushed by other objects, so its job is literally just to wake other bodies as it moves (which it does with the above changes)?

> PhysX has the best approach I have seen today. This is how I want speculative wakes to work, just waking for a frame or two to see if movement starts (not waking for the full time):

That's actually a really good idea for saving a little performance. More of something for a separate area, but yeah having a speculative wake and a collision wake as two separate types makes a lot of sense, with a different timer on each (I thought doing this by tick count made more sense BTW, I have a feeling I saw it measured in seconds, which is unnecessary afaik).

> It may make sense to consider the API again and make a specific WakeNeighbours function (rather than a flag). 

I've also considered this, it depends whether it would benefit all the backends, and whether some specific logic is needed per case to deal with this in the backend. However, having a timer as I mentioned above for the last move, then sending the `wake_neighbours` could be triggered from scene side potentially and fix all backends in this respect.

It depends really where we think the responsibility should lie. To be honest it's not a lot of code in the backends (a one liner or so), so I'm wavering whether there is a convincing need to add that new API .. it also leaves each backend free to handle it in the most efficient manner for it.

> UPDATE: Actually even better would be to use the "timer" approach I think I mentioned in an earlier post on this thread. Every time we move the static / kinematic, we store the current tick. If we try and move it and it has not been moved in the previous tick, we run wake_neighbours. This should catch nearly all cases and not impede efficiency for a continuous movement. So together with waking on disable / enable, this should catch all the current bugs I think.

Yes this would call wake_neighbours() less often. It is still a somewhat expensive function, but if you can make it less likely to be called en-masse then it's not a problem.

I am also equally ok to just let Bullet not 'wake on move away' or 'wake on free', since they are not as important as 'wake on move'. Then if someone raises the issue, it could be considered again.

I looked into trying to implement a faster wake_neighbours() within Bullet itself this morning, but it didn't seem to work the way I hoped. I think Bullet simply doesn't maintain the internal links for quickly doing this. I suspect Jolt doesn't also, and maybe PhysX...I think it depends on the architectural approach. 

> > It may make sense to consider the API again and make a specific WakeNeighbours function (rather than a flag).

> I've also considered this, it depends whether it would benefit all the backends, and whether some specific logic is needed per case to deal with this in the backend. However, having a timer as I mentioned above for the last move, then sending the wake_neighbours could be triggered from scene side potentially and fix all backends in this respect.

A wake_neighbours() function might benefit Jolt and Bullet (and maybe PhysX). I think GodotPhysics, Rapier and Box could just ignore it.

Godot Physics maintains a directly connected constraint graph like Box2D/3D, so IMO wake_neighbours() is cheap enough to fully automate. External engines like Rapier and Box already handle the 3 cases automatically.

I think at the end of the day, it is ok to let different engines do this differently, since they have different underlying architectures and purposes. If someone has a problem with Bullet or Jolt's approach, then they can choose GodotPhysics or Rapier or something or vice versa, or they can use the query API to handle waking edge cases the recommended way.

From Jolt README.md

> Accidental wake up of bodies cause performance problems when loading / unloading content. Therefore, bodies will not automatically wake up when created. Neighboring bodies will not be woken up when bodies are removed. This can be triggered manually if desired.

From Jolt Architecture.md
> Unlike some other physics engines, removing a Body from the world doesn't wake up any surrounding bodies. If you want this you can call BodyInterface::ActivateBodiesInAABox with the bounding box of the removed body (or the combined bounding box if you're removing multiple bodies). Also, things like setting the velocity through Body::SetLinearVelocity will not wake up the Body, use BodyInterface::SetLinearVelocity instead. 

So my thoughts are
* I think exposing a wake_neighbours() function with a default implementation that does nothing is ok. It could be a good helper for Jolt (as it could implement what Jolt docs recommend). It is unnecessary for some common engines (and wouldn't be necessary for Godot if we pursue some fixes).

* I think making Bullet handle all wake cases automatically in a performant way is tricky (to consider edge cases like level teardown), but the ideas you mentioned sound viable and a good compromise could be made that is viable for 3.x without bleeding into other SKU's. I wonder if a similar pattern of partly automating this might be good for Jolt.

* I think making Godot Physics handle all wake cases automatically is viable and should be done either way, to make the most of its simple architecture. I am happy to refine that PR across all Godot Physics SKU's.

I think the burning question for me right now is whether @jrouwe might have something to say on this. It would be helpful to know if there is a 'best approach' for Godot-Jolt.

I've just added the basic proof of concept version with the timer, before I have a look at `GodotPhysics` to see whether it will be worth combining them with a `wake_neighbors` API as you say. I've also updated the text in the PR description at the first post.

One thing I did notice that is potentially problematic with all the engines (and perhaps why Jolt used an AABB), is that in the MRP, when I pushed a box on top of the platform, then disabled the platform, the platform was no longer paired to the box, so didn't wake the box. Whereas if I let the box fall on the platform, didn't push it, then disabled the shape, it was paired, and therefore the box _did_ fall.

This suggests that in some cases, the current pairings are not enough, or are not reliable, at least for Bullet.

This may suggest that in the long run, it may be worth considering an expanded AABB wake function (like Jolt) for situations like deleting a body, or disabling a shape. However what is curious is that this problem _only_ seems to occur so far in the MRP when disabling the shape. I can't get it to occur when `queue_freeing` the platform, or when moving it totally outside the scene (i.e. everything works correctly).

For `GodotPhysics` BTW, the BVH uses margins on the AABBs, so this problem seems unlikely to happen. A box sitting on a platform should always end up paired with it (if I remember right, it's a long time since I wrote the BVH).

Godot physics testing:
- [x] Forward seems to work
- [ ] Deleting doesn't work
- [x] Moving platform away does work
- [ ] Disabling shapes doesn't work

I'll see if I can fix these via the equivalent `wake_neighbors` function in `GodotPhysics` (it already exists). I'm still slightly preferring the solution here that we fix them totally in the backend, rather than add a new API function for this, although I'm willing to be converted if there is a good argument.

Some things that I see problematic with an API function:
* It might be needed in some of the situations for one backend, and others in another backend (there's no specificity here)
* Adding an extra function call across the API isn't free if it goes across a queue, and we don't actually _need_ another function

UPDATE: I've fixed both these cases in `GodotPhysics`. Have also added you as co-author, @Schnorg .

I've left the "speculative wake" idea for a separate PR (perhaps you want to have a go at this).

I have to admit that I didn't read this entire thread, but w.r.t. waking up bodies when other bodies are sleeping: As you figured out already from the readme, we had a lot of performance problems with this. If an entire world chunk is streamed out, we have like 10K static bodies testing if there are dynamic bodies in the vicinity. We then wake up those bodies, only to remove them immediately after because those bodies are usually also part of the same chunk. This was causing frame stutters.

So my recommendation would be to make it explicit for the user to say that bodies in a certain area should be woken up and not attempt to do this automatically (or at least provide a way to opt out). You can make a helper function for waking the neighbors of a single body, but I think it is better to have a version that takes an aabb like Jolt has. This allows you to combine multiple bodies and activate the entire area at once. Alternatively, you could have an API that takes a list of bodies and let each physics engine figure out what the best way is.

I did suspect that we might benefit from some optimization for level loading / unloading, likely as a follow up. Your situation of a streaming world is an extreme example of this, which is good for stress testing.

My thoughts are this:

### Baseline
Physics should, as a baseline, be able to perform as you would expect real physics objects to behave. That is if you add / move an object into a situation touching other objects, it should wake them up, and when removing, it should also wake them up. This is what the PR offers. This should cover regular gameplay.

At the moment, the bodies just _don't behave as you would expect them too_, likely as performance hacks, leading to limitations on how you can use static / kinematic bodies.

### Branch loading / unloading
Level loading / unloading. We've had a number of issues with this in the past, such as physics objects getting all added at the origin, overloading the broadphase, _before_ they get moved to their initial position. Indeed there's an argument for not adding the physics bodies to the broadphase at all until they have their initial transform (aside from the special case where they are intended to be at the origin).

So perhaps we can fix loading and unloading with something like a simple system of physics bodies having deep sleep, or rather active / inactive status. When objects are loaded in, they could start inactive, then a branch could recursively set to active all physics objects after loading. Conversely, when deleting a branch, we could first recursively set all to inactive, _before_ deleting.

### Historical
It is notable that this kind of thing wasn't resolved when the engine was first put together. However it was probably written as a "small world" engine with a few objects and these considerations weren't engineered in from day 1.


### More work
I'll try some stress tests on loading / unloading, and test a simple active / inactive loading system. But I do suspect this should be a follow up, rather than feature creep in a single change.

#### Alive status
In fact it's possible we could consider the present behaviour of `static` and `kinematic` as "inactive", then have a method to set a branch to active, thus making the proper behaviour opt-in, if there are worries about backward compat / loading / saving performance.

#### Manual `wake_neighbors()` API
Alternatively, we could go back to @Schnorg 's idea of a specific `wake_neighbours()` API call and leave it to users to call that during adding / removing, if desired, for statics and kinematics? Maybe that would be simplest compromise, rather than have it happen automatically.

Otoh the movement system I think _should_ happen automatically (i.e. `Bullet` should match the current behaviour of `GodotPhysics`).

I'll try adding this as an alternative PR for comparison.
UPDATE: Done, see #124422.

I've also got a branch that tracks an `alive` status of bodies, and sets them to alive when entering / exiting the tree. However this doesn't solve the problem of `queue_free()` it turns out, because it's difficult to know whether an object has been removed during gameplay, or as part of unloading. So perhaps a manual call is a good compromise. :thinking: 

What do you guys think?

My view is currently tending towards trialling #124422 first, because a manual function may do the job, and if there is still demand for an auto-version, we can add this later, and the manual call will practically be a no-op. :thinking: 

It also may be better to call on demand actually for another reason:
The edge case currently in Bullet where sometimes pushing the box first gets rid of the pairing between the box and the platform. This may require a specific AABB check with an expanded AABB to be robust (I gather the `GodotPhysics` function does this already). The reason seems to be that Bullet may aggressively prune narrow phase pairings when it detects both objects are sleeping.

Ah I've realised a snag in the `Bullet` `wake_neighbors()` function, I'd assumed it was a pair cache per body, but it's not, it's a global pair cache, so even though it will work, it will be slow for high N because it will go through a bunch of pairings that aren't necessary.

So I think for `Bullet` I'd have to do something like the AABB test anyway. Or see if I can iterate through an island directly.

UPDATE: I've swapped to an AABB test in the other PR.
I'll close this one because on reflection I think it's probably better to call manually, we can continue discussion there.
